title: Participle clauses with adverbial meaning 1
subtitle: Opening her eyes, ... / Having finished the book, ...
summary: Use -ing, -ed, having + -ed and passive participle clauses to say when, why or on what condition something happened, and keep the implied subject right.

lesson.heading: What these clauses do
lesson.text: Present participle (-ing) and past participle (-ed) clauses can work like adverbials, giving information about the timing, the causes or the results of the event in the main clause.

examples.text: **Opening** her eyes, the baby began to cry.
**Faced** with a bill for £10,000, Ivan has taken an extra job.
**Looked after** carefully, the plant can live through the winter.

lesson.heading: The forms
rows: **Opening** her eyes, the baby began to cry.
**Faced** with a bill for £10,000, Ivan has taken an extra job.
**Having finished** the book, I had a holiday.
**Having been hunted** close to extinction, the rhino is once again common in this area.

lesson.heading: The implied subject
lesson.text: The subject of a participle clause is not stated: we understand it from the main clause, so it is usually the same as the subject of the main clause.

examples.text: **Arriving** at the party, we saw Ruth standing alone.
**Having wanted** to drive a train all his life, this was an opportunity not to be missed.
examples.note: here the implied subject (he) is not mentioned in the main clause at all

lesson.heading: Two different subjects: avoid it
lesson.text: In careful speech and writing we avoid a participle clause whose implied subject is different from the subject of the main clause - the result sounds absurd. Use a full clause instead.

examples.text: Turning round quickly, the door hit me in the face.
examples.note: first implied subject = I; second subject = the door

examples.text: **When I turned round quickly**, the door hit me in the face.

lesson.heading: A subject of its own
lesson.text: In formal English the participle clause can have its own subject, which is often a pronoun or includes one. An -ing clause of this kind describes something happening at the same time as the main event, or comments on the facts in the main clause.

examples.text: The collection of vases is priceless, **some** being over 2000 years old.
**Her voice** breaking with emotion, Vasiliki spoke about her father's illness.

lesson.heading: Where not goes
lesson.text: not usually comes before the participle, but it can follow it - and the position changes the meaning.

examples.text: **Not understanding** the rules, I found the cricket match boring.
examples.note: = because I didn't understand the rules

examples.text: **Hoping not** to be recognised, I chose a seat in a dark corner.
examples.note: = I hoped that I wouldn't be recognised

lesson.heading: having + -ed or plain -ing?

left.label: having + -ed: the main clause is the consequence
left.text: Use having + past participle when the main clause happens because of the earlier event.
examples: **Having broken** her leg the last time she went, Giorgia decided not to go on the school skiing trip this year.
**Having waited** six weeks for the washing machine to be delivered, I decided to cancel the order.

right.label: -ing: same time, or simply before
right.text: Either form works when the first action is finished before the second begins; -ing alone can also mean 'while'.
examples: **Taking off** his shoes, Ram walked into the house.
**Running** across the field, I fell and hurt my ankle.

lesson.note: 'Having run across the field, I fell ...' would mean I fell after I had crossed the field, not while crossing it.

lesson.text: Read your participle clause and the main clause subject together: if the subject cannot sensibly do the participle's action, rewrite the sentence with a full clause.

exercises.prompt: ___ quickly, I soon caught up with her.
exercises.explanation: = Because / While I was walking quickly. An active verb becomes an -ing clause.

exercises.prompt: ___ a nurse, she knew what to do after the accident.
exercises.explanation: = As she was a nurse. Being + noun gives the reason.

exercises.prompt: ___ where the theatre was, she asked for directions at the hotel reception.
exercises.explanation: not normally comes in front of the participle.

exercises.prompt: ___ his childhood in Oslo, he knew the city well.
exercises.explanation: The knowledge is the consequence of the earlier, completed event, so having + past participle.

exercises.prompt: ___ the day before for arriving late, I was eager to catch the bus in good time.
exercises.explanation: An earlier passive event that causes the main clause: having been + past participle.

exercises.prompt: Do the participle clause and the main clause have the same implied subject, or different subjects?

items.text: Known mainly as a writer of novels, Rashid has now written a successful biography.
Keeping a careful eye on the spider, Suzanne hurried out of the bathroom.
Found only in the Andes, the plant is used by local people to treat skin diseases.
Waiting for the bus, a car went through a puddle and splashed water all over me.
Looking down from the hill, the town spread out before us towards the coast.
Feeling rather sick, the boat ploughed through the huge waves.

exercises.prompt: ___ to cry, she waved to Harun as the train pulled out.
exercises.explanation: She was trying; what she tried not to do was cry - so not follows the participle.

exercises.prompt: ___ to put on his coat, he left the house.
exercises.explanation: Here the whole idea is negative (= he didn't bother), so not comes before the participle.

exercises.prompt: Match each participle clause with the main clause that follows it.

pairs.right: I don't yet have internet access.
I could see Ida running after me.
I banged my head on the low roof.

pairs.left: Having waited six weeks for the washing machine to be delivered,
pairs.right: I decided to cancel the order.

pairs.left: Having suffered from depression myself as a teenager,
pairs.right: I could understand how Nathan was feeling.

pairs.left: Having learnt some Swahili as a child,
pairs.right: I was able to understand most of what she said.

exercises.statement: Turning round quickly, the door hit me in the face.
exercises.explanation: When I turned round quickly, the door hit me in the face. The participle clause and the main clause need the same subject.

exercises.statement: Breaking her leg the last time she went, Giorgia decided not to go on the school skiing trip this year.
exercises.explanation: Having broken her leg the last time she went, Giorgia decided not to go ... The main clause is the consequence of the earlier event, so we need having + past participle.

exercises.prompt: Put this formal sentence in order. The participle clause has a subject of its own.
exercises.answer: Her voice breaking with emotion, Vasiliki spoke about her father's illness.
exercises.explanation: In formal English the participle clause can keep its own subject (her voice).
